  • Childhood obesity has immediate and long-term effects on physical, social, and emotional health.
  • Children with obesity are at higher risk of having other chronic health conditions and diseases that influence physical health. These include asthma, sleep apnea, bone and joint problems, type 2 diabetes, and risk factors for heart disease.
  • Children with obesity are more likely to suffer from social isolation, depression, and lower self-esteem.
  • In the long term, a child with obesity is more likely to have obesity as an adult..
  • An adult with obesity has a higher risk of developing heart disease, type 2 diabetes, metabolic syndrome, and many types of cancer

Obesity is a multifactorial disease. #22

  • Genetic bases of obesity is heterogeneous
  • Environmental factors are permissive to the development of the disease
  • Obesity susceptibility genes are neither sufficient nor necessary fat increase.
  • They only modulate in every individual the deleterious effects of environmental factors on the energy balance.

Polygenic obesity #23

  • Polygenic factors - group of common genes, which increases the susceptibility of weight gain, when present in certain forms
  • Contribution of genetic factors to weight gain - 30-70%
  • Mechanisms:
  • • regulate accumulation / distribution of adipose tissue
  • • regulate metabolic rate and its response to physical activity
  • • control the caloric intake and food selection

Candidate genes for obesity #24

  • Polymorphism of rs9930506 – FTO genes (fat mass- and obesity-associated gene)
  • FTO – expressed in numerous tissues (adipose, pancreas cells, scheletic muscles, cerebral tissue)
  • Frequency of alleles FTO inducing the risk for obesity in general population - 63%,
  • Population risk of FTO - 20%
  • C. Bala. Tratat de DNBM, vol 2, 2010
  • T. Rendo et al. Obes Facts 2009;2:393–399

Common variants near MC4R and FTO seem to have additive effects on BMI. #25

  • When comparing individuals with no risk alleles at either locus (19% of the population) with those homozygous at both (1%), the point estimate of the BMI difference amounts to ~1.17 kg/ m2 in adults.

Obesity pathogenesis involves two related but distinct processes: #30

  • (1) sustained positive energy balance (energy intake > Energy expenditure) and
  • (2) resetting of the body weight “set point” at an increased value.
  • The latter process explains why weight lost through changes of diet and/or lifestyle tends to be regained over time, a major obstacle to effective obesity treatment.
  • Endocrine Reviews 38: 267 – 296, 2017)

  • According to the first law of thermodynamics— obesity results from the imbalance between calories in and calories out.
  • Although that simple equation remains true, we now recognize the complexity of appetite regulation, physical activity patterns, eating behaviors, and the downstream consequences associated with obesity.

Slide 32 #32

  • Fundamentally, humans have an “evolutionary physiology” that is predisposed to conserve body fat (energy) as a factor of survival.
  • This evolutionary physiology in today’s climate of easy access to virtually unlimited calories has created a large segment of humanity that appears to be biologically predisposed to excessive weight gain.

Complex & Multifactorial Pathophysiology of Obesity. #39

  • Obesity is a complex disease with interactions involving genetic, environmental, biological, and behavioral factors that favor a positive energy balance.

Signals related to the fat mass are integrated with signals from the gastrointestinal system to control all aspects of energy homeostasis #41

  • Schwartz MW, Nature 2000;404:661-71

Notes: Signals such as leptin and insulin are secreted in proportion to the size of the fat mass and circulate in the blood. They enter the brain and act at the level of the hypothalamus. Neuroendocrine signals from the stomach, the gastrointestinal system and the liver are sent to the hindbrain, providing information about the food that is eaten: its taste and chemical content, and how much the stomach is distended.

Obesity - as a disorder of neurotransmission #43

  • Neurotransmitters and neuropeptides involved in the regulation of energy balance are altered in obesity
  • Alexandre Caron. The Journal of Clinical Endocrinology & Metabolism, 2021, Vol. 106, No. 12, e4872–e4886

Notes: The main hypothalamic nuclei, neuropeptides and pathways involved in the regulation of appetite. Circulating hormones act on the ARC, which has an incomplete blood-brain barrier and, hence, can affect downstream pathways, which modulate appetite control. In the ARC, orexigenic neurons coexpress NPY and AgRP, whereas neurons coexpressing POMC and CART are anorexigenic. In the ARC, activation of AMPK leads to increased food intake, an effect that is inhibited by insulin and leptin. AgRP = Agouti-related protein; AMPK = Adenosine monophosphate protein kinase; ARC = Arcuate nucleus; CART = Cocaine- and amphetamine-related transcript; CB1 = Endocannabinoid receptor 1; CCK = Cholecystokinin; DMN = Dorsomedial nucleus; GLP = Glucagon-like peptide; LHA = Lateral hypothalamic area; MCH = Melanin-concentrating hormone; NPY = Neuropeptide Y; OXM = Oxyntomodulin; POMC = Pro-opiomelanocortin; PYY = Peptide YY; PVN = Paraventricular nucleus; VMN = Ventromedial nucleus.

  • the homeostatic control of the long-term energy reserve and nutritional status in the body.
  • Leptin - secreted by white adipose tissue in proportion to the body’s fat mass.
  • Leptin and insulin bind to their respective receptors in the arcuate nucleus to decrease food intake and increase energy expenditure.
  • Leptin resistance - excessive adiposity

Notes: Signals such as leptin and insulin are secreted in proportion to the size of the fat mass and circulate in the blood. They enter the brain and act at the level of the hypothalamus. Practical Conclusion #73

  • Underlying medical conditions leading to the manifestation of obesity. :
  • - genetic, endocrine
  • - macro-environmental influencers (eg, 24-hour lifestyle, economic structure, global stressors),
  • - micro-environmental influencers (eg, eating schedules, physical activity, sleep health, drugs)
  • The ultimate consequence is failure of the homeostasis of weight and energy regulatory mechanisms, leading to an elevated body fat set-point.
  • Only when we recognize that obesity is a disease can we take the next steps of screening, diagnosing, assessing, preventing, and treating this condition.
